title: What Does Pro Rata Mean in Salary? A Guide to Hourly to Annual Conversion
description: Understand what pro rata means in salary and how to convert your hourly rate to annual pay using a 38-hour week. Includes tax, super, and Fair Work definitions.
salarySummary: Assuming a 38-hour week, your annual salary is your hourly rate multiplied by 1,976 hours (38 × 52).

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52. For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual salary before tax and super.

faqs.q: What does pro rata mean in salary for part-time workers?
faqs.a: Pro rata means a proportionate amount. Part-time employees receive entitlements (like annual leave and personal leave) based on the hours they work compared to a full-time employee. For example, if a full-time worker earns $60,000 for 38 hours per week, a part-time employee working 19 hours per week would receive a pro-rata salary of $30,000.

faqs.q: Is casual loading included in the hourly rate for annual conversion?
faqs.a: No. Casual loading (usually 25%) is paid on top of the base hourly rate. When converting to annual salary, use the base hourly rate without casual loading. The loading is additional pay for casual employees to compensate for lack of leave entitlements.

bodyMarkdown:
## What Does Pro Rata Mean in Salary?

If you are moving between jobs or negotiating a pay rise, you may have heard the term "pro rata" and wondered what it means for your salary. In Australian workplaces, pro rata simply means a proportionate amount. The Fair Work Ombudsman defines it as "a proportionate amount of money or period of time." Part-time employees generally get pro-rata entitlements based on the number of hours they work compared to a full-time employee.

When you are converting an hourly rate to an annual salary, understanding pro rata helps you compare offers fairly. This guide explains the standard formula, how to handle part-time and casual work, and what tax and superannuation mean for your take-home pay.

## The Standard Conversion Formula

The basic formula to estimate your annual salary from an hourly rate is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time employee under most awards, the standard week is 38 hours. So the calculation becomes:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, if your hourly rate is $30.00:
- Weekly pay = $30.00 × 38 = $1,140.00
- Fortnightly pay = $1,140.00 × 2 = $2,280.00
- Annual gross pay = $1,140.00 × 52 = $59,280.00

This method assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It is a starting point for comparing job offers.

## Pro Rata for Part-Time Employees

If you work part-time, your salary is calculated pro rata. That means you receive a fraction of the full-time salary based on your hours. For instance, if a full-time role pays $70,000 for 38 hours per week, and you work 20 hours per week, your pro-rata salary is:

$70,000 × (20 ÷ 38) = $36,842.11

You can also use the hourly rate method: multiply your hourly rate by your actual weekly hours and by 52. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that part-time employees generally get pro-rata entitlements, meaning your leave and other benefits are also proportional.

## Minimum Wage and Award Rates

Australia has a National Minimum Wage set by the Fair Work Commission. From 1 July 2026, the minimum wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making their minimum rate $33.05 per hour. Most industries also have award rates that may be higher. You can check the latest [pay guides](/blog) for your award.

When converting an award rate to annual salary, use the base hourly rate without casual loading. The loading is paid on top of the base rate and is not part of the annualised salary calculation.

## Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees get a loading (usually 25%) to compensate for not receiving paid leave. If you are casual, your hourly rate is higher, but your annual salary estimate should still use the base rate. For example, if your casual rate is $33.05 (including loading), the base rate is $26.44. Use $26.44 × 38 × 52 to estimate annual earnings.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. The super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27). So if your annual gross is $60,000, your employer must add $7,200 to your super fund. This is not part of your take-home pay but is an important part of your total compensation.

## Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual salary is taxed using the resident tax rates for 2026–27:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income. The Australian Taxation Office sets the thresholds. For this estimate, we use the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds.

To estimate your take-home pay, subtract tax and Medicare from your gross annual salary. Remember that this is an estimate only. Your actual tax may vary due to deductions, offsets, or the Medicare levy surcharge.

## Using the Timesheet Calculator

Our [timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading. It calculates your weekly, fortnightly, and annual pay, then estimates tax and super. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading – use the checkbox to add it on top.

For more detailed comparisons, see our [reference tables](/data) for award rates and average earnings.

## Summary

Understanding what pro rata means in salary helps you negotiate fair pay whether you work full-time, part-time, or casually. The standard conversion uses hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For part-time workers, pro rata ensures you receive a fair proportion of full-time entitlements. Always check your award or enterprise agreement for the correct minimum rates, and remember that super is paid on top of your salary.
